newsitem.title: USA: Churning still a threat to unwary investors.
newsitem.headline: Churning still a threat to unwary investors.

text.p: Churning -- the practice of excessive trading to garner commissions -- continues to plague some brokerage clients.

Despite the recent growth of of fee-based financial advice and the popularity of buy-and-hold investing, there are still some unsavory brokers bilking their clients out of thousands of dollars in commissions.

According to San Diego attorney John Lawrence Allen, who makes a living representing clients who have been wronged by brokers, stock market gains have fuelled more feverish trading by brokers whose clients could have made more by buying and holding.

Two brothers who had a small business turned $700,000 over to a broker they didn't know very well. In just 18 months they spent almost $400,000 in commissions. The broker turned their entire account over 10 times, almost 10 times as much as the typical mutual fund manager might turn over a portfolio.
Allen has other colourful stories that may make you feel sorry for his ripped off clients, or may, in some cases, leave you feeling like they should have known better.

Like the man who borrowed $115,000 on a home equity line of credit to redo his house, and then turned the whole sum over to a broker to "make some money" while he was waiting for the contractor to start on the job. By the time the contractor showed up, the money had been wiped out, so he sent the contractor home.

Another client, a busy physician, invested $100,000 with a broker who would call him several times a day to get approval for trades. Finally the doctor said, "I'm busy, just do what you want." The next time he checked, he only had 8 cents left on the dollar.
What do these victims have in common? Greed, sure.

But laziness, too, and the belief that somebody they don't even know can be trusted to make them rich in a hurry. All of them discovered problems in their accounts when it was too late -- their brokers called and told them they had to ante up more money to meet margin calls.
You can avoid such scenarios with a bit of care.
Check every trade and every statement, and add up the commissions that your account is creating. If your broker starts making more than you are, look out!

Remember, too, that state-of-the-art investment theory maintains that the less you trade, the better. Stock market winners buy and hold and reapportion their portfolios among stocks, international stocks and bonds, maybe once a year.
Even active mutual fund managers rarely turn over an entire portfolio more than once a year.

According to Allen, case law says that if your portfolio changes more than twice a year, there's an inference that your broker was churning. If it turns over more than four times a year, the broker has to prove he wasn't churning. And if your holdings change six times in one year, existing cases have held this was "conclusive" evidence of churning, Allen said.

Any excessive trading can help make your broker rich on wild rides when the market moves up fast enough to cover his excesses and your bad judgment. Once the market calms down, the trading will be exposed as the money-loser it was.
Unfortunately, most people don't sit up and take notice until it's too late. But that's when Allen gets really busy, with more and more cases to file and clients to comfort.
